subtype: Approach: asking why it hurts so much [Thinking]
passage: In their Kolkata flat, Trisha sat on the bed with her knees pulled up. For a week a boy in her class, Ujjwal, had been calling her drawings "baby scribbles", and today he'd said it in front of the art teacher's table. Her mother had already phoned the class teacher that afternoon, and the teacher had promised to speak to Ujjwal the next morning. Still, Trisha couldn't stop replaying it. Her mother sat beside her. "Which word hurts most?" Trisha thought. "Baby. Because... I'm scared he's right. That I'm not good." "Is he right?" Trisha looked at the wall covered with her drawings: the owl, the rain market. "The art teacher put my owl on the board." She was quiet for a while. "He doesn't get to decide what I am." It still stung, but smaller.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal call Trisha's drawings?
qa.a: "Baby scribbles".

qa.q: Why did the word 'baby' hurt Trisha most?
qa.a: She was scared he was right and that she is not good, so the word touched her own insecurity.

qa.q: What else could help Trisha when the words keep replaying?
qa.a: Looking at real evidence, like the owl on the board, and telling her mother or teacher if the comments continue.

qa.q: How does Trisha's mother handle it?
qa.a: She has already phoned the teacher, and then asks questions instead of giving answers, so Trisha reaches the thought herself.

grounding: A girl asks herself which words hurt and why, and with her mother's questions decides the bully's opinion does not define her while adults act.

subtype: Approach: asking why it hurts so much [Thinking]
passage:
"Nu, why do I keep crying about it? She only said I talk funny."
"Which words, exactly, Siami?"
"That I sound like a cartoon. That nobody understands my Hindi."
"Which part hurts most?"
Lalremsiami thought. "The 'nobody'. Like I don't belong here."
"Do you believe it?"
"...Priya understands me. And Ma'am. And I got a star for my speech."
"So is 'nobody' true?"
"No." She wiped her face. "Sarita's words are about Sarita, not about me."
"That's your thought, not mine. And I spoke to your teacher after school today. She'll talk to Sarita tomorrow."
"Okay. It still hurts. But smaller."

qa.q: What did Sarita say Lalremsiami sounds like?
qa.a: A cartoon.

qa.q: Which word hurt Lalremsiami most, and why?
qa.a: 'Nobody', because it made her feel excluded, as if she doesn't belong.

qa.q: What else could Lalremsiami do if the comments continue?
qa.a: Tell her teacher the same day and remind herself of the real evidence: Priya, Ma'am and the star.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami's mother help?
qa.a: She asks questions so Lalremsiami finds her own answer, and she has already spoken to the teacher that day.

grounding: With her mother's questions, a girl works out which words hurt and why, and decides the bully's words do not define her while adults act.

subtype: Approach: choosing the right moment and mood [Thinking]
passage: Asif did his homework at the back of the waiting room of his father's small clinic, as he did every weekday. Yash's sleepover was on Saturday, and the question had been sitting in his throat all afternoon. At five the room was full: a crying baby, an old man coughing, the phone ringing. His father came out twice, rubbing his forehead, and took a call standing in the corridor. "Not now," Asif thought. "If I ask now, I'll get the tired answer." He waited. At home after dinner, his father leaned back with his tea and started talking about a cricket match. Asif slid in beside him. "Abbu, Yash has invited me to sleep over on Saturday. His parents will be home. Can I go?"

qa.q: Where did Asif do his homework?
qa.a: At the back of the waiting room of his father's clinic.

qa.q: What was Asif thinking when he decided 'Not now'?
qa.a: He was worried that a tired, busy father would say no, so he chose to wait for a calmer mood.

qa.q: What else could Asif add when he asks?
qa.a: The details Abbu might want, such as Yash's parents' number, so the decision is easy.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel being asked after dinner?
qa.a: Relaxed and more ready to listen than he was in the rush of the clinic.

grounding: A boy waits for his father to relax after dinner before asking about a sleepover, instead of asking at a tired, busy moment.

subtype: Approach: choosing the right moment and mood [Thinking]
passage: I'm Divyansh, and I was at Tanvir's house when he asked about the sleepover. His father came home at seven still on a work call, pacing and saying, "No, no, the delivery..." Tanvir started to get up, then sat down again. At dinner his father was quiet and kept checking his phone. Tanvir passed him the dal and said nothing. Later his father put the phone on the charger, stretched and laughed at something on the television. That's when Tanvir went and sat on the arm of his chair. "Papa, can I sleep over at Divyansh's on Friday? His mother said yes." His father said, "Let me call her, but probably yes." I don't know if Tanvir planned it, but it looked like he was waiting for something.

qa.q: What was Tanvir's father doing when he came home?
qa.a: Still on a work call, pacing.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir have sat down again when his father came in?
qa.a: He probably felt it was a bad moment and was nervous that a distracted father would say no.

qa.q: What else could Tanvir do if his father stays busy all evening?
qa.a: Ask the next morning at breakfast, or leave a short note, rather than catching him mid-call.

qa.q: How does Divyansh read Tanvir's timing?
qa.a: Divyansh isn't sure it was planned, but thinks Tanvir was waiting for something.

grounding: A friend watches a boy hold back his sleepover request until his father has finished work and relaxed.

subtype: Approach: preparing reasons and answers to objections [Action]
passage:
Monday: Trisha wanted a bicycle more than anything, but last time she'd asked, her parents had said "Why?" and she'd said "Because." This time she opened a notebook with her friend Keerthana. Page 1: WHY. School is a twenty-minute walk; tuition is across the main road.
Wednesday: Page 2: SAFETY. Helmet, only the colony lanes and the back road, never the highway, lights for evenings. Page 3: MONEY. Her birthday money, and watering Mrs Iyer's plants on weekends for a little extra. Keerthana played Papa: "What if it rains?" Trisha added a line.
Saturday: At breakfast Trisha asked. For every question Papa raised, she had a page. He looked at Amma, then said, "Let's go and look at some on Sunday."

qa.q: How long is Trisha's walk to school?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt at breakfast on Saturday?
qa.a: Nervous, but confident because she had a page ready for every question.

qa.q: What else could Trisha offer to make the yes easier?
qa.a: A trial month with her safety rules, so her parents can see the plan working before fully agreeing.

qa.q: How might Papa see the notebook?
qa.a: Papa is likely impressed that she thought about safety and cost, which makes it easier to say yes.

grounding: Across a week, a girl prepares reasons, safety rules and how she will help with the cost before asking for a bicycle.

subtype: Approach: preparing reasons and answers to objections [Action]
passage: Vaibhav, you just said "please" twelve times. Let me tell you how I, Devika, got my first bicycle. I was eleven, one of the few girls in our town who wanted one. My father said no twice. So I sat under the neem tree with a slate and wrote down my reasons like a lawyer. One: school was three kilometres away, and my mother was tired of walking me. Two: I'd ride only on the canal road, where there were no buses. Three: I'd put in my Diwali money and sell guavas from our tree to the neighbours. Then I thought of what he would say, "What if you fall?", and wrote: "I'll learn in the school ground first." When I read it to him, he laughed, then went quiet. The next month, a green bicycle stood by the door.

qa.q: How far away was the school?
qa.a: Three kilometres.

qa.q: How did young Devika feel after her father said no twice?
qa.a: Probably disappointed, but determined enough to prepare a proper case.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference?
qa.a: Writing her reasons and answering her father's likely worry, 'What if you fall?', before he could ask it.

qa.q: How did Devika's father react when she read the slate?
qa.a: He laughed, then went quiet, as if impressed and thinking it over seriously.

grounding: An elder recalls preparing reasons, a safety plan and a way to help pay before asking her father for a bicycle.

subtype: Approach: nagging and repeating the demand [Pitfall]
passage: At the parent-teacher meeting, Wasim's mother had just sat down in front of Mrs Menon when Wasim started again. "Everyone in my class has a phone. Please, Ammi, please." It was the eleventh day in a row. He had asked at breakfast, in the auto, at dinner, and now here, in the classroom, with other parents waiting. When his mother shook her head, his eyes filled and his voice got loud. Mrs Menon looked up. Wasim's mother said quietly, "We never said never. But every time he cries, it's harder to even think about it." On the way out she told him, "No phone talk for a month." Wasim kicked the gate. Before the meeting, the answer had been "not yet". Now it was a month of nothing.

qa.q: How many days in a row had Wasim asked?
qa.a: Eleven days.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when his eyes filled?
qa.a: Frustrated and upset, desperate for a yes.

qa.q: What other approach might have worked better for Wasim?
qa.a: Asking once, calmly, with his reasons and how he would use a phone, and accepting 'not yet' as a real answer.

qa.q: How does Wasim's mother experience the pressure?
qa.a: She finds the crying makes it harder even to think about a phone, so she becomes firmer.

grounding: A child who nags and cries for a phone every day makes his mother firmer, turning 'not yet' into a month of no.

subtype: Approach: nagging and repeating the demand [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Charu, Madhav's older sister. For two weeks Madhav has asked Papa for a phone every single day. First at breakfast. Then when Papa came home, before he'd even taken his shoes off. Then through the bathroom door. When Papa said no, Madhav cried loudly, and once threw his school bag. He never said what he needed the phone for, only "I want it" and "You never give me anything." At first Papa said, "Maybe for your birthday." Last night Papa said, "Now the answer is no until next year." Madhav looked shocked. I think he really believed that asking more would work. I don't know what he's feeling today; he hasn't said a word about phones at all.

qa.q: How long has Madhav been asking for a phone?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: What might Madhav be feeling after Papa's new answer?
qa.a: Shocked, and perhaps regretful that asking more made things worse.

qa.q: What else could Madhav have tried?
qa.a: Explaining what he needs a phone for and agreeing to wait for his birthday with some rules.

qa.q: How does Charu see what happened?
qa.a: Charu thinks Madhav believed nagging would work, and notices his silence about phones today.

grounding: A sister watches a child's daily nagging and crying for a phone turn a 'maybe' into a firm no.

subtype: Approach: offering something in exchange [Action]
passage:
Saturday
Tonight I made my offer. I didn't beg this time. I wrote it on a sheet like a real deal: If we get a dog, 1) I, Darshan, will take him for the morning walk before school, every day, even in the rain. 2) My marks will stay at least where they are now. 3) If I miss the walk three times in a month, we talk again. Gautam-bhaiya said number 3 was clever because it shows I'm serious. Papa read it twice. Mummy asked, "Who walks him when you have a school trip?" I hadn't thought of that. Bhaiya said he'd do those days. Papa said they'd think about it for a week. A week is not a no!
Darshan

qa.q: What does Darshan promise to do before school?
qa.a: Take the dog for the morning walk every day, even in the rain.

qa.q: How does Darshan feel about Papa's answer?
qa.a: Hopeful, even excited, since 'a week is not a no'.

qa.q: What else could Darshan add to the offer?
qa.a: A plan for other gaps, like feeding when the family is away, worked out with Papa and Mummy.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the deal?
qa.a: Mummy seems to take it seriously, since she looks for gaps like school trips rather than refusing.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child offering a clear exchange, walks and steady marks, in return for having a dog.

subtype: Approach: offering something in exchange [Action]
passage: In their village near Sangli, a stray puppy had followed Darshan home along the school path three days running. On the fourth day he didn't beg Aai to keep it. He waited until she was sorting rice on the verandah and sat beside her with his school diary. "Aai, if we keep her, I'll walk her to the fields and back every morning before school. And my marks won't drop. You can check my diary every Friday." His sister Pooja added, "I'll feed her when he has cricket." Aai kept sorting. "And if your marks drop?" "Then she goes to live with Pooja's friend's family," Darshan said, swallowing hard. Aai looked at the puppy, then at him. "One month. Show me."

qa.q: When did Darshan sit beside Aai?
qa.a: While she was sorting rice on the verandah.

qa.q: What does Darshan swallowing hard suggest?
qa.a: He felt nervous; the consequence was hard to say, but he wanted to show he was serious.

qa.q: What else could Darshan offer Aai?
qa.a: A weekly check with her on the walks as well as the marks, so she sees the whole deal working.

qa.q: How does Aai see the deal?
qa.a: Aai takes it seriously and gives a one-month trial to see if Darshan keeps it.

grounding: A boy offers daily walks and steady marks in exchange for keeping a puppy, giving his mother a fair deal to try.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing the request with a sibling [Thinking]
passage: In their Jaipur flat, Rajni cornered her older brother Aakash on the terrace. "Be Papa. I'm going to ask about the Shalini trip." Aakash folded his arms and frowned exactly like their father. "Hm?" "Papa, Shalini's family is going to Pushkar on Saturday and they've asked me. Everyone's going." "Everyone? Name them." Rajni stopped. "Well... Shalini." "Weak," said Aakash, dropping the frown. "Try again." She thought. "Papa, Shalini's parents are driving, they'll be with us all day, we're back by seven, and Aunty said you can call her." Aakash frowned again. "And your homework?" "Done on Friday." Aakash grinned. "That one might actually work." Rajni wrote the second version on her palm.

qa.q: Where is Shalini's family going?
qa.a: To Pushkar on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when Aakash said 'Name them'?
qa.a: Caught out and a little embarrassed, realising 'everyone' was a weak argument.

qa.q: What else could Rajni prepare before asking Papa?
qa.a: She could ask Shalini's mother to call Papa, since hearing it from the adult in charge may reassure him most.

qa.q: How does Aakash see the practice?
qa.a: Aakash enjoys playing Papa and seems pleased when the second version sounds convincing.

grounding: A girl rehearses asking for a trip with her older brother playing the strict father and learns which arguments sound weak.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing the request with a sibling [Thinking]
passage:
"Unni-chettan, pretend you're Achan."
"Fine." Her brother put on a pair of reading glasses. "Yes, Gopika?"
"Achan, Vasudha and four girls are going to the beach next Sunday. Can I go? Please, please, please."
"Who is driving?"
"Umm... someone's mother."
"Someone?" Unni took off the glasses. "He'll say no in two seconds. 'Please' isn't a reason."
Gopika chewed her pen. "Okay. Again." She sat up straighter. "Achan, Vasudha's mother is driving and staying with us. We'll swim only between the lifeguard flags. I'll call you at lunch and when we leave. We're back by six."
Unni put the glasses back on. "And if it rains?"
"Then we go to Vasudha's house instead."
"...Achan might say yes to that."

qa.q: Where are the girls going next Sunday?
qa.a: To the beach.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after Unni's first feedback?
qa.a: A little deflated, chewing her pen, then determined to try again.

qa.q: What else could Gopika do before asking Achan?
qa.a: Ask Vasudha's mother to speak to Achan directly, since an adult's word may settle his worries.

qa.q: How does Unni-chettan help Gopika?
qa.a: By acting strict, Unni shows which parts of her request would sound weak to Achan.

grounding: A girl practises asking for a beach trip on her older brother, who plays their father, and replaces weak reasons with clear ones.

subtype: Approach: accepting a no and asking what would change it [Revision]
passage: Yogesh, you slammed the door because your Amma said no to the late show? When I was twelve, I did the same. My friends were going to the fair after dark, and my Abba said no. I, Farhan, slammed the door so hard the calendar fell off the wall. Then I sat on my bed and thought: slamming has never got me anything. So I went back and asked, quietly, "Abba, what would I need to show you to get a yes next time?" He looked surprised. Then he said, "Come home on time from small things first. Tuition, cricket, the market. Show me you're where you say you are." For two months I was home five minutes early from everything. At Eid, when my friends went to the late fair, he said yes.

qa.q: What fell when young Farhan slammed the door?
qa.a: The calendar fell off the wall.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling as he sat on the bed?
qa.a: Farhan calmed down and felt a little foolish, seeing that slamming had never helped.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference?
qa.a: Asking calmly what would earn a yes, then coming home early from small outings for two months.

qa.q: How might Abba have felt when Farhan asked calmly?
qa.a: Surprised and probably respected, which made him give a clear, fair answer.

grounding: An elder recalls accepting a no, calmly asking what would change it, and earning trust through smaller outings.

subtype: Approach: accepting a no and asking what would change it [Revision]
passage: Arnab's friends were already downstairs, ringing a cycle bell, when his mother said no. "Not the nine o'clock show at the mall, Arnab. You're twelve." The bell rang again. Arnab felt the old anger rising, the urge to argue or sulk. Instead he took a breath. "Okay. Not tonight. But Ma, what would I need to show you so it's a yes some day?" Elizabeth blinked, then sat down on the arm of the sofa. "Honestly? That you come back when you say. Start with the afternoon show. Call me when it ends. Do that a few times." Arnab nodded, ran down, told his friends he'd join the four o'clock show on Sunday instead, and wrote "afternoon show, call Ma" on the back of his hand.

qa.q: Which show did Arnab want to go to?
qa.a: The nine o'clock show at the mall.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when his mother said no?
qa.a: Angry; the old urge to argue or sulk rose up before he took a breath.

qa.q: What else could Arnab do to build trust sooner?
qa.a: Keep every small promise, like calling after the afternoon show, so his mother sees a pattern quickly.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth react to the calm question?
qa.a: Elizabeth was surprised, sat down and gave an honest, clear answer.

grounding: With friends waiting, a boy accepts his mother's no and calmly asks what would earn a yes, getting a clear first step.

subtype: Approach: asking a grandparent to speak first [Action]
passage:
Tuesday
It worked, sort of. On Sunday I told Granny about the art classes at the community hall and asked if she could bring it up first, because when Granny says something, Mum and Dad actually stop and listen. Tonight at dinner Granny said, "That child draws on every scrap of paper in this house. Have you seen the art classes near the library?" Dad put down his fork. Then I said my part, the one I'd practised: the classes are on Saturdays, so no school is missed, my friend Yusuf's sister goes, and I'd give up TV on Saturday mornings. Mum said she'd call the hall tomorrow and ask about the fee. Granny winked at me across the table.
Elizabeth

qa.q: When are the art classes?
qa.a: On Saturdays.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when Granny winked?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt hopeful and supported, pleased that the plan was working. 😊

qa.q: What else could Elizabeth do if the fee turns out to be a problem?
qa.a: Talk it over with Mum and Dad and ask the hall about other options, rather than giving up.

qa.q: How does Granny seem to experience her part?
qa.a: Granny enjoys it, winking across the table, glad to help.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child asking a grandparent to raise the idea of art classes first, then adding reasons at dinner.

subtype: Approach: asking a grandparent to speak first [Action]
passage: In their kasba near Amritsar, a retired drawing teacher had started art classes in the gurdwara hall on Sunday afternoons. Jaya wanted to go more than anything, but her father always called drawing "time-pass". So on Thursday, while Dadi was shelling peas in the courtyard, Jaya sat beside her. "Dadi, will you tell Papa about the classes first? He always listens to you." Dadi smiled. At dinner on Friday Dadi said, "Gurleen's mother says the drawing classes are good. Our Jaya's hands are always busy with a pencil." Papa grunted. Then Jaya spoke clearly: "It's only Sunday afternoons, after my homework. Gurleen is going too. And I'll help Dadi with the peas first." Papa looked at Dadi, then at Jaya. "Try it for a month."

qa.q: Where are the classes held?
qa.a: In the gurdwara hall on Sunday afternoons.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel about asking Papa directly?
qa.a: Nervous, since Papa always calls drawing 'time-pass'.

qa.q: What else could Jaya do if Papa had said no?
qa.a: Show him her drawings and ask what would change his mind, keeping Dadi on her side.

qa.q: How does Papa respond?
qa.a: He grunts at first, then, after hearing both Dadi and Jaya, agrees to a month's trial.

grounding: A girl asks her grandmother to mention art classes first, since her father listens to her, and then adds her own reasons.

subtype: Approach: hiding the request and doing it anyway [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday night
Worst day. I knew Papa would say no to the big park across the highway, so I didn't ask. I told Mummy I was going to Sachin's, and Sachin and I cycled to the far park instead. It was great for an hour. Then Sachin's uncle saw us at the traffic signal and called Papa. When I got home Papa didn't shout. That was worse. He just said, "Now when you say you're at Sachin's, how will I know?" Tonight I asked if I could go to the cricket camp next week, and he said "We'll see" in the voice that means no. I think I made everything harder, not just today.
Santosh

qa.q: Who saw Santosh at the traffic signal?
qa.a: Sachin's uncle.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel tonight?
qa.a: Regretful and worried, sensing that one hidden trip has made every future request harder.

qa.q: What else could Santosh have done?
qa.a: Asked Papa, accepted a no, or suggested going with an adult, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How might Papa feel now?
qa.a: Hurt and unsure whether he can trust what Santosh says, which shows in his quiet disappointment.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child who cycled to a far park without asking, lost the parents' trust and found later requests harder.

subtype: Approach: hiding the request and doing it anyway [Pitfall]
passage: Kishore was sure Baba would say no to the river, so he didn't ask. On Saturday afternoon he told his sister Aditi he was going to the library in the next village, then pedalled the other way, down the dust road to the ghat where the older boys swam. He didn't swim; he just watched and skipped stones. But the milk-van driver passed him on the bridge and mentioned it to Baba at the dairy. That evening Baba sat on the charpai and asked, "Library, Kishore?" Kishore looked at his feet. Baba said only, "I would have said no to swimming. But I might have said yes to watching, with your uncle." A week later, when Kishore asked to go to the fair in town with friends, Baba said no without even thinking.

qa.q: Where did Kishore say he was going?
qa.a: To the library in the next village.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when Baba asked 'Library, Kishore?'
qa.a: Ashamed, looking at his feet.

qa.q: What else could Kishore have done?
qa.a: Asked Baba openly; he might have been allowed to watch at the river with his uncle.

qa.q: What might Aditi feel about being told the library story?
qa.a: Aditi was used as part of the cover story, so she may feel uncomfortable or hurt once she learns the truth.

grounding: A boy goes to the river without asking, expecting a no, is found out and loses his father's trust for later requests.

subtype: Approach: writing a short letter when speaking feels hard [Action]
passage: The week Hansa wanted to ask, her parents were busy with Binita-masi's wedding, and the house was full of relatives and noise. Every time Hansa opened her mouth at dinner, someone else started talking, and she lost her nerve anyway. So on Tuesday night she tore a page from her notebook and wrote slowly: "Dear Mummy and Papa, the school is starting a swimming class on Saturday mornings. I want to join because I can't swim and I feel scared near water. There is a coach and a lifeguard. I will not miss any tuition. You don't have to answer now." She folded it and slipped it under Papa's spectacles case. Two days later, in the middle of the wedding chaos, Mummy squeezed her hand and whispered, "We read it. Yes."

qa.q: When is the swimming class?
qa.a: On Saturday mornings.

qa.q: Why did Hansa choose to write a note?
qa.a: She felt shy and kept losing her nerve in the noisy house, so writing felt safer.

qa.q: What else could Hansa have done to be heard?
qa.a: She could have asked Binita-masi or another relative to help her find a quiet moment with her parents.

qa.q: How might Hansa's parents experience the note?
qa.a: They had time to read it and think without pressure, even in the wedding chaos, before saying yes.

grounding: In a busy, noisy week, a shy girl writes her parents a polite note about joining swimming, giving them time to decide.

subtype: Approach: writing a short letter when speaking feels hard [Action]
passage: Dilnaz practised the question in the mirror three times, and each time her throat closed up. Her parents weren't strict, but whenever she had to ask for something, her face burned. So after homework, in their Pune flat, she wrote on a sheet of blue paper: "Ammi and Abbu, my friend Leela's building has a swimming class on Sundays, 8 to 9. I'd like to join because I love water and want to swim properly, not just splash. It's near, and Leela's mother can walk us. Please think about it. You can tell me whenever you're ready." She stuck it on the fridge with the mango magnet and went to bed early. In the morning there was a second note under hers in Abbu's handwriting: "Thank you for telling us so clearly. Let's see the pool on Sunday."

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz stick the note?
qa.a: On the fridge, with the mango magnet.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when trying to ask aloud?
qa.a: Shy and nervous; her throat closed up and her face burned.

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz try if a note didn't work?
qa.a: Ask Leela's mother to mention the class to her parents, so the idea reaches them from an adult too.

qa.q: How does Abbu respond?
qa.a: With a calm note of his own, thanking her and suggesting they see the pool on Sunday. 🙂

grounding: A shy girl writes a polite note about joining a swimming class and leaves it for her parents to consider without pressure.
